Hello
I have some questions about a CoYoneda-like theorem of mine that
I have proved, agreed, with with some help of AI.
I have already a post about the theorem that can be found in
the AI authored projects channel (it has been moved to it from
the general channel).

I am going to remove the post from AI authored projects where
more challenging (Collatz-like) proofs are discussed.

In this post I also put a link to the complete code
because of my questions about it relate to Mathlib.
Including the code made the post to long to publish

https://github.com/LucDuponcheelAtGitHub/coEndoYoneda/blob/main/CoEndoYoneda.lean

So here are some questions

  1. The proofs are very explicit and do not use catdish
    (they use grind twice). Maybe both catdish and grind
    can be used more times?

  2. Is this the kind of theorem that, eventually, can make it
    into Mathlib?

  3. I know that the standard (Co)Yoneda code in Mathlib has
    many more (Co)Yoneda related defs lemmas and theorems.
    My code is a "proof of concept", for now only proving
    coEndoYonedaEquiv, which is similar to coyonedaEquiv.
    Frankly, I'd love to become a Mathlib contributor with
    my own invented CoYoneda-like theorem.

Unless this would really help existing material (which is unlikely), this is probably not in the scope of mathlib right now.

FYI I looked at your file and it doesnt contain much documentation in the file itself (like a useful header), which would make the code much easier to understand.

Felix, no problem.

About the motivation

given a presheaf C ⥤ Type u and a functor Type u ⥤ C
they can be composed to an endofunctor C ⥤ C

such a functor Type u ⥤ C exists, of course, when C = Type u,
the world of "pure functions without side-effects"

but what about the world of "programs" that consist both of
"pure functions without side-effects" and
"impure functions with side-effects"?

so my idea was to formulate a (co)yoneda lemma for endofunctors
that could play a role in the programming world

and, yes, I was able to find necessary conditions,
monadic natural transformations for global-like elements,
and I was able to prove a coyoneda-like equivalence

but, FYI, there is more (bad news and good news)

first the bad news

trying to find out if Kleisli morphisms of type KleisliCat M
for a monad M satisfy my necessary conditions, it
turned out that the answer was : no, they don't

so my coyoneda-like equivalence is not useful for the
programming world, only for the "pure programming" world,
as far as KleisliCat M is concerned, where "pureness" then
boils down to "monadic computation referential transparancy"
(cfr "expression evaluation referential transparancy")

now the good news
(every disadvantage has an advantage)

my necessary conditions actually classify the property
of being "pure", without "side-effects" in KleisliCat M
in a categorical way, because they force equality
mz >>= fun z => pure (pure z) = pure mz in KleisliCat M
which, by the way, can be proved in Lean

in a nutshell, as a side-effect (no pun intended (!)) I proved,
in the KleisliCat M world the following theorem

*Referential transparancy is exactly the condition required for
a computational context to admit a global coyoneda endofunctor
equivalence*
